content: I am a graduate student at Michigan State University in the Geospatial Lab of Dr. Andrew Finley. My research interests lie in the development of Bayesian hierarchical models for environmental monitoring and decision making. More specifically, I am interested in the development and application of statistical models for methods of monitoring wildlife populations across large spatio-temporal regions, including citizen science data and acoustic recordings.

Flexibility This feature can be used for publishing content such as:
 Online courses Project or software documentation Tutorials  The courses folder may be renamed. For example, we can rename it to docs for software/project documentation or tutorials for creating an online course.
Delete tutorials To remove these pages, delete the courses folder and see below to delete the associated menu link.
Update site menu After renaming or deleting the courses folder, you may wish to update any [[main]] menu links to it by editing your menu configuration at config/_default/menus.toml.
For example, if you delete this folder, you can remove the following from your menu configuration:
[[main]] name = "Courses" url = "courses/" weight = 50  Or, if you are creating a software documentation site, you can rename the courses folder to docs and update the associated Courses menu configuration to:
[[main]] name = "Docs" url = "docs/" weight = 50  Update the docs menu If you use the docs layout, note that the name of the menu in the front matter should be in the form [menu.X] where X is the folder name. Hence, if you rename the courses/example/ folder, you should also rename the menu definitions in the front matter of files within courses/example/ from [menu.example] to [menu.<NewFolderName>].

summary: Modeling the diameter distribution of trees in forest stands is a frequent application in ecology that supports key biologically and economically relevant management decisions. The choice of model used to represent the diameter distribution and how to estimate its parameters has received much attention in the forestry literature; however, accessible software that facilitates comprehensive comparison of the myriad modeling approaches is not available. To this end, we developed an R package called `ForestFit` that simplifies estimation of common probability distributions used to model tree diameter distributions, including the two- and three-parameter Weibull distributions, Johnson’s SB distribution, Birnbaum-Saunders distribution, and finite mixture distributions. Frequentist and Bayesian techniques are provided for individual tree diameter data, as well as grouped data. Additional functionality facilitates fitting curves to height-diameter data. The package also provides a set of functions for computing probability distributions and simulating random realizations from common finite mixture models.
title: ForestFit: An R package for modeling plant size distributions

content:
The use of acoustic data in ecological and environmental studies has seen a dramatic increase over the last 20 years with the growth of the fields of ecoacoustics and soundscape ecology. This has largely been the result of technological developments enabling researchers to purchase large amounts of relatively inexpensive autonomous acoustic recording units. While ecoacoustics and soundscape ecology are rapidly expanding to help inform our understanding of how organisms use the acoustic environment and how this relationship is influenced by anthropogenic activities, the development of occupancy modeling techniques for acoustic data is still in it’s infancy. Acoustic recordings are ideal for large-scale wildlife monitoring studies to help inform trends in occupancy across large spatial areas over time as they are inexpensive, easy to implement, non-intrusive, and provide a permanent record that can be used later for further studies if desired. Further, with the development of clustering algorithms to identify individual bird songs in acoustic recordings, acoustic data could be a valuable source when it comes to monitoring avian species’ ranges and distributions. Thus, combining acoustic recordings, clustering algorithms, and occupancy modeling techniques could provide a very efficient system for monitoring acoustically active wildlife over extended periods of space and time.
I seek to extend upon previous work on single-season, single-species occupancy models for acoustic data and develop a dynamic, multispecies (community), spatially explicit occupancy model utilizing acoustic data to estimate trends in species occupancy across possibly large spatio-temporal regions. The model will require a combination of an automated clustering algorithm to cluster similar sounds into groups, an expert ornithologist to identify what species these groups represent, and then small amounts of manual validation of individual songs within each group. The extension of the basic single-season, single species occupancy model to a dynamic, community, spatially-explicit occupancy model will greatly expand the applicability of acoustic recordings in wildlife monitoring programs seeking to monitor trends in occupancy in a large number of species across vast spatio-temporal regions.

content:
The Northeast Temperate Inventory and Monitoring Network (NETN) of the National Park Service (NPS) consists of 13 parks in the Northeastern United States. As breeding landbirds are important components of park ecosystems and are very popular among park visitors, the NETN has implmented a volunteer-based breeding landbird monitoring program over the last 13 years to provide insight on the trends of the avian communities in each of these parks. Volunteer birders collect data using traditional point-count surveys, where they mark each bird they observe, estimate how far they are from the bird, and record the time of the first sighting of each individual bird. Because this is a volunteer based survey, we require a protocol that is not too labor intensive for the volunteers, while also enabling estimation of population trends of important species of interest. The NETN protocol enables estimation of avian abundance and trends over time through the use of removal sampling and distance sampling models to account for each observer not detecting every bird present at a given point count location. Because many important birds of interest are not highly abundant across the parks, we seek to use a multi-species (or community) model to enable inference on such rare species and not focus solely on the common species that we could estimate using a single-species model. We also seek to share information across the parks in the NETN system, as some parks are better monitored than others. We are currently in development of a multi-region, community, dynamic removal sampling model to provide inference on the status and trends of important landbird species in the Northeastern United States. Specifically, we seek to
 Determine the rate of change in abundance of important avian species of interest in each NETN park. Develop a multi-region, community, dynamic abundance model to provide inference for all species and all parks across a large geographical area. Determine the influence of silvicultural practices and habitat variables on avian abundance.
summary: Developing efficient models to assess changes in breeding landbird populations in NETN parks.
title: Breeding Landbird Monitoring in Northeast Temperate Network parks

from IPython.core.display import Image Image('https://www.python.org/static/community_logos/python-logo-master-v3-TM-flattened.png')  print("Welcome to Academic!")  Welcome to Academic!  Install Python and Jupyter Install Anaconda which includes Python 3 and Jupyter notebook.
Otherwise, for advanced users, install Jupyter notebook with pip3 install jupyter.
Create a new blog post as usual Run the following commands in your Terminal, substituting <MY_WEBSITE_FOLDER> and my-post with the file path to your Academic website folder and a name for your blog post (without spaces), respectively:
cd <MY_WEBSITE_FOLDER> hugo new --kind post post/my-post cd <MY_WEBSITE_FOLDER>/content/post/my-post/  Create or upload a Jupyter notebook Run the following command to start Jupyter within your new blog post folder. Then create a new Jupyter notebook (New > Python Notebook) or upload a notebook.
jupyter notebook  Convert notebook to Markdown jupyter nbconvert Untitled.ipynb --to markdown --NbConvertApp.output_files_dir=. # Copy the contents of Untitled.md and append it to index.md: cat Untitled.md | tee -a index.md # Remove the temporary file: rm Untitled.md  Edit your post metadata Open index.md in your text editor and edit the title etc. in the front matter according to your preference.
To set a featured image, place an image named featured into your post’s folder.
For other tips, such as using math, see the guide on writing content with Academic.
summary: Learn how to blog in Academic using Jupyter notebooks
title: Display Jupyter Notebooks with Academic

porridge = "blueberry" if porridge == "blueberry": print("Eating...")  Math In-line math: $x + y = z$

$$ f\left( x \right) = \;\frac{{2\left( {x + 4} \right)\left( {x - 4} \right)}}{{\left( {x + 4} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}} $$

The basic simple linear regression model is ubiquitous in ecology. The model takes the following form:
\[ y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + e \\ e \sim (0, \sigma^2) \]
where \(y\) is the dependent response variable and \(x\) is the independent explanatory variable. The first step to do prior to performing a linear regression should be to plot \(y\) versus \(x\) to confirm a linear relationship between the variables exists.
\(\beta_0\) is the y-intercept and \(\beta_1\) is the change in unit \(y\) for a change in unit \(x\).
There are numerous ways to estimate the regression parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), but of course the most common method to use is called Least Squares Estimation. Remember the crucial assumption of least squares estimation:
\[ e_i \sim IID(0, \sigma^2) \]
for all \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\). Note that for actually estimating the parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) you do not need to assume normality of the errors, but if you wish to do any sort of hypothesis testing than you do need to.
The idea behind least squares estimation is to minimize the sum of squares of the residuals:
\[ \sum_{i = 1}^ne_i^2 = \sum_{i = 1}^n(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1x_i)^2 \]

content:
In this document I provide some details to potentially help clarify the concept of “repeated measures”. I have often found these sorts of experimental design terms to be very confusing. Here I hope to clarify the concept of repeated measures as a method to account for temporal autocorrelation in a dataset.
Repeated measures designs are a specific type of design where there is some sort of temporal autocorrelation among data points. Specifically, in a repeated measures design it is assumed that the same individual study units (e.g., trees) are measured at multiple time points. Thus, from an experimental design standpoint, one can view individuals as being a blocking variable and the variation within the subject represents the experimental error. Thinking hierarchically, we can imagine our full set of data points in a regression where at the second level there is a random effect of “individual”, where these are 0-centered normally distributed variables with a single variance, where that variance is said to account for the similarity among individuals.
This sort of example I just discussed where the subjects that are repatedly measured over time are treated as a blocking variable (i.e., random effect) is the most basic sort of repeated measures design. In fact, this has a special name, and is referred to as Compound Symmetry. You can also view this as saying that “observations within a subject are equally correlated with each other”. This most basic type of repeated measures design can be summed up in the following basic hierarchical model:
\[ \begin{aligned} y_{ij} \mid \omega_j &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu + \mu_i + \omega_j, \sigma^2) \\ \omega_j &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau^2) \end{aligned} \]
From this hierarchical model, it is clear how this most basic repeated measures design works (which is also equivalent to a basic RCBD with the blocking factor being random). It is also clear from this hierarchical perspective the variance components incorporated in the measurements for each individual measurement.
Key Point: repeated measures designs are extensions of a basic random effects model that provides more structure of how data points within a blocking variable are related to each other. Repeated measures are simply a method to account for non-indenpendence of data points that specifically has to do with temporal autocorrelation.
Let’s next consider some other basic autocorrelation structures.
AR(1) The AR(1) covariance structure is very commonly used in time-series applications. One important thing to consider is that the AR(1) requires equally spaced intervals of time. The covariance structure takes the following form:
\[ \sigma^2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho & \rho^2 & \rho^3 & \dots \\ \rho & 1 & \rho & \rho^2 & \dots \\ \rho^2 & \rho & 1 & \rho & \dots \\ \rho^3 & \rho^2 & \rho & 1 & \dots \end{pmatrix} \]
Notice how this structure assumes constant variance among the observations. In an hierarchical model, one can consider the structure of the model to take the following form for any given set of values \(\boldsymbol{y}\) that come from the same group that is repeatedly measured over time.
\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{y}_j \mid \boldsymbol{\omega}_j &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu + \boldsymbol{\mu}_j + \boldsymbol{\omega}_j, \text{diag}(\sigma^2)) \\ \boldsymbol{\omega}_j &\sim \text{Normal}(\boldsymbol{0}, \tau^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\rho)) \end{aligned} \]
where \(\tau^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\rho)\) is equivalent to the AR(1) covariance structure defined above.
There are numerous other covariance structures that can be assumed depending on the structure one thinks can be reasonable for the data.
 Double Repeated Measures Now let’s consider the situation where one expects temporal autocorrelation over two separate time periods. In other words, there are two units of time where repeated measures take place, and it is not reasonable to group these into a single time unit.
This is actually exactly analogous to what you did in your first publication. This concept would be a double repeated measures where you have an unstructured covariance matrix for the time of day, and then an AR(1) covariance matrix for the 29 minute recordings.

Here I provide some useful commands for using vi.
Commenting out a Block of Code Go to first line you want to comment: press ctrl v. This puts you in the Visual Block mode. Use the arrow key and select until the last line. Press Shift i, which puts the editor in Insert mode and then press #. This will add a hash to the first line Press Esc.   Copying text to the global clipboard "+y "+p To copy the entire file into the + register, gg"+yG   Moving around Move cursor to top of screen: gg Move cursor to bottom: shift + g Move cursot to end of current line: g_ Move to the beginning of line: 0
